# The Problem: Secrets, Teams, and Untrusted Servers

FOKS, the Federated Open Key Store, is a system for storing secrets and
sharing them within teams, with a server in the middle that is not trusted to
read the data or to tell the truth about who holds which keys. This chapter
states that problem precisely, because every technique in the rest of the book
exists to solve one piece of it.

## What users want

A person or a team wants to keep three kinds of data:

- **Key-value data.** Passwords, API tokens, configuration files, and larger
  binary files, organized into directories, readable and writable from
  several devices.
- **Team structure.** Who is in the team, with what role, and which devices
  they use. Membership changes over time: people join, leave, and get
  promoted; devices are added and lost.
- **Messages.** Real-time chat within a team.

They want this to work across devices they own, to survive the loss of any one
device, and to be usable by both humans and automated tools. They also want
the system to be *federated*: a team on one host should be able to include
users whose accounts live on another host, the way email works across
providers.

## What the server may not learn or do

The defining design decision of FOKS is that the server is treated as an
adversary with a very specific set of powers. It stores and relays data, and it
is honest enough to stay online, but it is assumed capable of reading anything
it stores and of returning whatever it likes to any request. The system is
built so that, even then, two guarantees hold.

**Confidentiality.** The server never holds a key that decrypts user data. It
sees ciphertext, the sizes and timing of requests, public keys, and
commitments to names. It does not see file names, directory shapes, file
contents, or chat text. Part II of this book is about how the keys that
provide this guarantee are created, derived, shared, rotated, and recovered.

**Integrity of history.** The server cannot invent a device, add a member to
a team, or roll a user back to an earlier set of keys without every client
noticing. Every change to an identity or team is a signed entry in an
append-only chain, and the server publishes a signed summary of all chains
in a Merkle tree, so that a client can check that what it is shown is
consistent with what everyone else is shown. Part III is about those chains,
the tree, and the checks clients perform.

Stating the threat model as "what the server can and cannot do" is useful
because it draws the line clearly. The table below is the line FOKS draws.

| The server can | The server cannot |
|---|---|
| See usernames and host names as commitments, device IDs, and public keys | Read stored secrets, file contents, directory names, or chat messages |
| See the size and timing of every request and stored object | Learn the structure of a directory tree beyond entry counts |
| Order changes into epochs and publish signed roots | Forge a change to an identity or team, which requires a device signature |
| Refuse service, rate-limit, or go offline | Present an old state to a client that has seen a newer one without detection |
| Store and forward invitations and encrypted key parcels | Open a key parcel, which is encrypted to the recipient's device |

The last row of the "cannot" column is the subtle one. Detecting rollback
requires the client to remember what it has already seen and to refuse to go
backwards. That memory, and the rules for advancing it, are the subject of
[Chapter 13](13-client-verification.qmd).

## What the server is trusted for

No design removes trust entirely. FOKS still relies on the server for
availability, for ordering (the server decides which of two concurrent
changes comes first), and for delivery of key parcels and invitations. A
malicious server can deny service, and it can *withhold* a change from one
client while showing it to another, at least until the client compares notes
with someone else. The book is careful to say what is and is not detected;
FOKS as implemented in `foks-rs` gives each client a consistent view of its
own history but does not include a gossip protocol between clients.

## Constraints that shape the solution

Several further requirements shape the design more than the threat model
alone would.

**No master password.** Human-chosen passwords are weak and reused, and a
password typed into a phishing page is lost. FOKS accounts are anchored in
device keys instead. Losing every device is handled by a printed recovery
phrase with real entropy behind it, and adding a device is handled by a
short pairing code. [Chapter 6](06-hesp.qmd) covers both.

**Post-removal secrecy.** When a device is revoked or a member leaves,
the departed party must not be able to read anything stored afterwards, but
the remaining members must keep reading everything stored before. (The
repository calls this "forward secrecy"; [Chapter 5](05-generations.qmd)
explains why the book uses a narrower term.) This
requires *generational* keys: a fresh secret for each membership change, with
a way to reach older secrets from newer ones. [Chapter 5](05-generations.qmd)
describes the construction.

**Post-quantum resistance.** Data encrypted today may be recorded and
decrypted years later by a quantum computer that breaks elliptic-curve
cryptography. Every public-key encryption in FOKS therefore combines a
classical key agreement with a lattice-based key encapsulation mechanism, so
that both must fall before any ciphertext does. [Chapter 4](04-hybrid-encryption.qmd)
explains the hybrid construction.

**Hardware keys.** Some users want their signing key to live on a physical
token that never releases it. That imposes a different signature algorithm
and different curve than the software default, and the system must handle
teams whose members use a mix. [Chapter 7](07-hardware-keys.qmd) covers the
consequences.

**Byte-for-byte compatibility.** `foks-rs` is a reimplementation of a Go
program, and clients and servers of the two implementations must
interoperate. Signatures are computed over encoded bytes, so the encoding must
be canonical and identical across implementations, and even the reference
implementation's mistakes must be reproduced. [Chapter 9](09-canonical-encoding.qmd)
and [Chapter 23](23-compatibility.qmd) cover the encoding and the testing that
enforces the match.

**A single server should be simple to run.** The reference implementation
uses PostgreSQL. The Rust server uses one SQLite file with a single writer
and concurrent readers, trading peak write throughput for simpler operation.
[Chapter 18](18-server-storage.qmd) describes the resulting design.

**Crashes and retries.** Devices lose power mid-operation, and network calls
time out after the server has already applied the change. Operations that
publish randomness or allocate sequence numbers must be resumable without
duplicating effects. [Chapter 19](19-agent.qmd) and [Chapter 21](21-mcp.qmd)
describe the journaling and idempotency techniques used.

## Two chains

One organizing idea recurs throughout the book, so it is worth naming here.
FOKS keeps two independent structures per identity or team.

The **secrecy chain** answers "who can decrypt this?" It runs from a
device's private key, through the encrypted key parcel for the current
generation, back through a chain of older generation seeds, down to the
per-application keys that encrypt files and messages.

The **authority chain** answers "who authorized this change?" It runs from
a device's signing key, through a signed link in an append-only chain,
into a leaf of the server's Merkle tree, and finally into the pin a client
stores locally.

The two chains use different primitives, are verified separately, and fail
independently. Compromising a signing key lets an attacker append to the
authority chain but not read data; obtaining a decryption key lets an attacker
read data but not change membership. Part II follows the secrecy chain
downward; Part III follows the authority chain upward.

## Where to look

- `README.md` and `docs/GUIDE.html` in the `foks-rs` repository state the
  project's own threat model and design goals.
- The upstream Go implementation, `github.com/foks-proj/go-foks`, is the
  protocol's reference and the target of compatibility testing.

## Further reading

- Ross Anderson, *Security Engineering*, 3rd edition, Wiley, 2020, chapter 5
  (cryptography) and chapter 6 (access control), https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~rja14/book.html
- Nikita Borisov, Ian Goldberg, and Eric Brewer, *Off-the-Record Communication,
  or, Why Not to Use PGP*, WPES, 2004, https://otr.cypherpunks.ca/otr-wpes.pdf
  (an early statement of forward secrecy goals for messaging)
- Nik Unger et al., *SoK: Secure Messaging*, IEEE Symposium on Security and
  Privacy, 2015, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7163029
- Keybase, *Keybase Book: Server Trust*, https://book.keybase.io/docs/server
  (a closely related system with the same "untrusted server" stance)
- Marcela Melara et al., *CONIKS: Bringing Key Transparency to End Users*,
  USENIX Security, 2015, https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity15/technical-sessions/presentation/melara
